To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ionic form of the estrogen receptor from rat uterus and from human breast carcinoma can be changed by the presence of a proteolytic enzyme in the cytosol.
the estrogen receptor from rat uterus and from human breast carcinoma exists in two ionic forms and that a protease in the cytosol is involved in generating the second ionic form.

a cation dependent protease is present in the cytoplasm of rat uteri and in human breast carcinoma cells, and that this protease is responsible for the conversion of the ionic form of the estrogen receptor from rat uterus to a smaller ionic form of this hormone receptor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of estrogen receptors in human breast cancer.
the mechanism of estrogen receptor degradation.
a cation-dependent, protease-mediated degradation of estrogen receptor to a smaller species in both rat uterine and human breast cancer cytosols.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the estrogen receptor in human breast carcinoma and rat uterus is present in two ionic forms, a larger form and a smaller form which has a smaller apparent molecular size and which is cation dependent.
estrogen receptors exist as two distinct forms in both rat uterine and human breast carcinoma cytosols.

estrogen receptors from rat uteruses and human breast carcinomas are present in two ionic species: the first ionic form is a larger molecular weight species which is present in cytosol after short incubation times and is cation-independent and is not degraded by cation-dependent proteases; the second ionic form is present in cytoplasmic fractions after longer incubation times and in the presence of cations and is degraded by a cation-dependent cytosolic protease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
estrogen receptor in rat uterine and human breast carcinoma cytosols has two ionic forms.
the estrogen receptors from rat uterus are more stable than are estrogen receptors from human breast carcinoma.
the ionic form of the estrogen receptor from rat uterus and from human breast carcinoma is a proteolytically labile protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the second ionic form is not the result of a conformational change, but rather the result of proteolytic degradation.
the second ionic form is a protease-degraded form of the receptor and that the first ionic form is not a protease-degradated form.
the second ionic form was present in both rat uterine and human breast carcinoma cytosols.
